title: Shooting glasses and lens colours
summary: Why glasses are compulsory in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, how they protect, what yellow, orange, purple and smoke lenses are for, and what to do if you need prescription glasses.

body.html: Shooting glasses protect your eyes from target fragments, bouncing pellets, twigs and dust. In FITASC competitions they are compulsory, and a shooter who comes to the stand without them is treated as absent. Who else must wear them differs a little between the disciplines.

html.sporting: Shooters, referees, staff and anyone close to a stand must wear safety glasses, with no exceptions.
html.compak: Competitors, referees and staff must wear protective eyewear.

body.html: Impact resistance comes first. Shooting lenses are made of polycarbonate or similar materials that do not shatter, and good frames also cover the eyes from the side. Ordinary sunglasses are not good enough. Look for an eye protection standard mark: in Europe usually EN 166, in the USA ANSI Z87.1.

Lens colour will not make you a better shot, but it can help you see the target against a particular background. Many shooters use yellow in dull weather, fog and at dusk, and orange as an all-rounder. Purple can make an orange target brighter against trees and grass, and grey smoke cuts brightness in strong sun without changing colours.

There are also clear lenses for very dark weather and evening light. Colour is about comfort; protection comes from the impact-resistant lens. For a beginner, glasses with interchangeable lenses are enough: clear or light yellow plus one darker lens. Shoot first, notice in which light you struggle, then add lenses.

Shooting glasses have a special shape. When you mount the gun, your head tilts slightly onto the stock and you look through the upper part of the lens. That is why frames have a high bridge (the part that rests on your nose) and large lenses, so that your field of view is not cut off.

If you wear glasses for your eyesight, there are two main routes. One is shooting glasses with prescription lenses, ordered from an optician who knows sports eyewear. The other is a frame with a separate prescription insert behind interchangeable tinted lenses.
Everyday glasses are suitable only if their lenses are certified as impact-resistant and correct your distance vision. Discuss the choice with an eye doctor or optician before you buy.
A shooter looks at a target in the distance, so sharp distance vision matters most. From about the age of 40 many people develop presbyopia: close-up vision gets harder and the bead may blur.
Many coaches say this matters less than it seems, because your eyes should be on the target, not on the bead.

Have your eyes checked regularly, especially if targets have become harder to see at dusk or in bright light. If you start missing to one side as you get older, it is also worth rechecking your master eye: see Master eye and cross-dominance.

key_points.html: Glasses are compulsory; without them a shooter is treated as absent.
Lenses must be impact-resistant, with a protection standard mark.
Many shooters use yellow in dull light, orange as an all-rounder, purple against greenery and smoke in bright sun.
With a prescription: prescription shooting lenses or an insert behind the lens.
From about 40, have your eyes checked regularly.

did_you_know.html: The right lens colour also depends on your own eyes: two shooters on the same stand may pick different lenses and both be right.

quiz.q: Which lens suits bright sun when you do not want colours changed?
quiz.explain: A grey smoke lens cuts brightness without changing colours.

quiz.q: Why are ordinary sunglasses not suitable for shooting?

options.text: They may not stop a fragment or pellet
They are banned for their dark colour
They are too light to stay in place
They make targets look too small

quiz.explain: Shooting lenses are impact-resistant and carry an eye protection standard mark.

quiz.q: What do many shooters use a yellow lens for?

options.text: For bright sun in the middle of the day
To make the target look bigger
For contrast in dull light and at dusk
To protect the eyes from recoil

quiz.explain: A yellow lens can boost contrast when light is poor.
